objects: exposure X; outcome Y; observed polygenic scores
assumptions: polygenic scores capture only part of heritability
conclusion: Incomplete genetic adjustment by observed polygenic scores motivates extrapolation to heritability-based sensitivity scenarios.
span: However, because polygenic scores capture only a small part of heritability, controlling for polygenic scores cannot entirely capture genetic confounding. We therefore propose a sensitivity analysis using polygenic scores to gauge how likely it is that genetic confounding accounts, in part or entirely, for a given exposure-outcome association.

objects: G; X; Y; linear structural equation model
conclusion: Gsens represents genetic confounding by genetic factors influencing both the exposure and outcome in a linear structural equation model.
scope: The score measures genetic factors; latent extensions represent heritability.
span: We assume a linear structural equation model framework [32]. Akin to third variable confounding, genetic confounding is represented in Fig 3A: genetic factors (G)–here measured by polygenic score(s)–influence both the exposure (X) and the outcome (Y).

objects: genotyped cohort; exposure and outcome measurements
conclusion: Gsens fits a structural equation model to the matrix of observed correlations among polygenic scores, exposure and outcomes.
scope: The SEM uses observed correlations among scores, exposure and outcome and externally supplied heritability scenarios.
span: The estimation of βXY is based on the matrix of observed correlations between polygenic scores, exposure and outcomes. We then fit a Structural Equation Model to this matrix of correlations that aims to reflect the true extent of genetic confounding (see Methods).

objects: observed G; latent G*; heritability scenario
conclusion: Sensitivity analysis fits a structural equation model with a latent genetic variable to correct the observed score as an imperfect measure of heritability.
scope: The latent model extrapolates beyond variance explained by the observed score; no numerical optimizer or convergence guarantee is stated here.
span: In the sensitivity analysis, a structural equation model is fitted with a latent variable G* representing heritability, as presented in Fig 5. This can be understood as correcting for measurement error, i.e. G being an imperfect measure of G*. Genetic confounding estimated under this model reflects heritability under the chosen scenario rather than only what is captured by the polygenic score.

objects: standardized paths; variances; cross-path and residual association signs
conclusion: Optional constraints restrict paths and variances to feasible ranges and prevent cross-paths and residual associations from reversing sign.
scope: These are parameter-range constraints reflecting prior beliefs, rather than a specified probability prior or penalized objective; the paper cautions that constraints may artificially reduce standard errors.
span: The constrained models therefore impose constraints on parameters to avoid impossible values (standardized paths above one and negative variances) and implausible values (cross-paths and residual associations flipping sign). While these models fit the observed data less well than the unconstrained models, they accommodate our prior beliefs about the plausible range of parameter values.

assumptions: single-score linear model with observed standardized associations
conclusion: The adjusted association is beta_XY = (r_XY - r_GX r_GY)/(1 - r_GX^2), representing the residual association net of genetic confounding.
scope: Genetically mediated causal effects remain in the residual association.
span: β_{X Y} = ( r_{X Y} − r_{G X} r_{G Y} ) / ( 1 − r_{G X}^{2} ) (1) where βXY is the adjusted effect and r denotes observed standardized associations. Details are presented in Section B in S1 Text. Importantly, βXY corresponds to the standardized association between X and Y minus genetic confounding, i.e. the residual association between X and Y net of genetic confounding.

conclusion: Gsens assumes that the polygenic score is the true genetic value plus classical measurement error.
scope: This may fail with epistasis or gene-environment interactions.
span: Gsens assumes that the polygenic score reflects the true genetic value plus classical measurement error. This assumption would hold under an additive model but not necessarily under interactions (epistasis or gene-environment interactions).

objects: genetic and non-genetic confounders; conditioning on X
assumptions: non-genetic confounding; especially a score predicting X more strongly than Y
conclusion: Conditioning on the exposure can induce collider bias and amplify rather than reduce bias in the residual association.
scope: Adjustment need not improve on the observational association.
span: However, these estimates are biased by the association between genetic and non-genetic confounders induced by conditioning on the exposure X, an instance of collider bias (see Methods). The bias is most pronounced when adjusting for polygenic scores that explain more variation in X than in Y, and may lead to estimates of residual association that are more biased than the observational association, a phenomenon termed bias amplification [6].

assumptions: same trait in parent and child; constant heritability across generations; complete genetic confounding
conclusion: Under complete genetic confounding for the same parent-child trait with constant heritability, the model gives r_XY = 0.5 h_y^2.
scope: A model-based identity and consistency benchmark, rather than an unconditional causal identification or calibration theorem.
span: When the adjusted effect of X on Y is null, then rXY is equal to genetic effects through G. In the special case where X and Y are the same trait in parent and child and assuming constant heritability across generations, we thus obtain: r_{X Y} = 0.5 * sqrt(( h_{y}^{2} )) sqrt(( h_{y}^{2} )) = 0.5 h_{y}^{2} (3)

objects: mediation; confounding; indirect effect beta_XG beta_GY
conclusion: Gsens uses the statistical equivalence of mediation and confounding to estimate genetic confounding by treating the score as a mediator.
scope: This is a statistical representation; the germline score is not conceptually a mediator of a later exposure.
span: MacKinnon et al. demonstrated that mediation and confounding are statistically identical in linear structural equation modelling [33]. Therefore, genetic confounding can be estimated by treating the confounder–here the polygenic score G–as a mediator of the effect of X and Y (Fig 3B). The confounding effect is the indirect effect of X on Y through G: βXGβGY.

objects: genetic overlap; residual association; mediated and unmediated pleiotropy
assumptions: comparison with bivariate twin and mixed-model decomposition
conclusion: Gsens targets genetic confounding, whereas bivariate twin and mixed-model decompositions remove genetic overlap including effects mediated by the exposure.
scope: The estimands differ even when both use genetic information.
span: In twin-based methods, the corresponding residual association is an environmental association in that it excludes all genetic components from the observed association, including those mediated by the causal effect. In contrast, Gsens aims to remove only the genetic confounding or unmediated pleiotropy.

objects: Gsens; latent causal variable model; confounder effects
conclusion: Gsens and LCV both estimate genetic confounding parameters without identifying the causal exposure effect, while LCV emphasizes relative confounder effects on exposure and outcome.
scope: Conceptual similarity; no equivalence of models or estimates is asserted.
span: We note that a conceptually similar approach to ours is taken in the latent causal variable (LCV) model [27], which also estimates genetic confounding parameters without identifying the causal effect of the exposure. The emphasis of LCV is however on comparing the genetic confounder effects on the risk factor to those on the outcome.

objects: Gsens residual association; MR causal effect
assumptions: causal interpretation of the Gsens residual requires no non-genetic confounding
conclusion: MR imposes stronger genetic-confounding assumptions for causal identification, while Gsens cannot identify the causal effect from the residual association without assuming no non-genetic confounding.
scope: Comparative identification statement, rather than a finite-sample precision theorem.
span: Mendelian Randomization (MR) methods impose stronger assumptions on the genetic confounding effects to explicitly identify the causal effects [28]. In comparison with MR and LCV methods, our approach retains much of the precision of the observational association. However we cannot identify the causal effect from the residual association, unless we assume no non-genetic confounding.
